sections.heading: Admitting I cannot love as you command
sections.text: Father, you call me to love you with everything I am—my heart, my desires, my thoughts, my strength—and to love my neighbor as I love myself. I know this is right, and I want it to be true of me. But I also know I do not have this kind of love in myself. Left to myself, my loves bend away from you. I get tangled up in cravings, self-protection, pride, and comfort. You are completely worthy of my love, but I cannot give you pure love unless you rescue and free my heart.
theological_themes: God commands wholehearted love for himself and genuine love for neighbor.
Human love is disordered by sin and cannot make itself pure without God’s freeing grace.
Confession of moral inability is not an excuse but an honest dependence on God.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus identifies love for God and love for neighbor as the heart of God’s commandments. This grounds the prayer’s opening desire to love God wholly and people rightly.
Paul teaches that the mind set on the flesh is hostile to God and cannot submit to him. That supports the prayer’s confession that natural affections, apart from grace, do not freely love God.

sections.heading: Standing in the freedom Jesus has given me
sections.text: Thank you that, by your grace, I am no longer owned by sin. I belong to you. I believe you are my God because of Jesus, and through him you have bought me back, forgiven my sins, and made me free to serve you. I do not want freedom so I can live for myself. I want to obey you as your redeemed child.
theological_themes: Freedom from sin comes through Christ, not self-improvement.
Redemption and forgiveness create willing service to God.
Christian obedience flows from grace, not from an attempt to earn acceptance.

scripture_references.connection: This passage joins redemption through Christ’s blood with the forgiveness of sins according to God’s grace. It directly supports the prayer’s confidence that forgiveness and freedom are received through Jesus.
Paul describes Christ as the one who sets his people free. The prayer’s desire to serve God as a freed person rests on that gospel freedom rather than on self-generated righteousness.

sections.heading: Depending on your Spirit to walk in that freedom
sections.text: Lord, the same way I could not free myself in the beginning, I cannot live faithfully now by my own strength. Please let your Spirit draw me close to you, make your ways attractive to me, and teach me to walk in the freedom you have already given. Keep me from treating your grace as something I can carry without you.
theological_themes: The Christian life continues by dependence on the Spirit.
Obedience is the fruit of grace, not the achievement of independent strength.
True liberty is walking with God, not self-rule.

scripture_references.connection: Paul warns that Christian freedom is not an opening for self-indulgence but a call to love and to walk by the Spirit. This fits the prayer’s request to live freely in obedience rather than return to bondage.
Jesus teaches that his disciples can bear fruit only by abiding in him. The prayer’s dependence on God for ongoing obedience reflects that same need for continual life from Christ.

sections.heading: Using your Word to bring me to you
sections.text: Father, keep every practice, habit, and help in my life pointed toward you. If something does not lead me nearer to you, it will leave me empty no matter how religious it looks. Shape my steps by your Word. Teach me to receive your commands not as a burden but as a path into fellowship with you. Make obedience a place where I meet you, hear you, and learn to enjoy you.
theological_themes: Spiritual means are valuable because they lead to communion with God.
Scripture orders the believer’s life and directs the heart toward God.
God’s commandments are meant to become joy, not mere external pressure.

scripture_references.connection: The psalmist asks God to lead him in the path of God’s commandments and turn his heart away from worthless things. This supports the prayer’s desire for God’s Word to order life and make obedience joyful.
Jesus connects love for him with keeping his commandments and with his self-disclosure to the believer. That grounds the prayer’s hope that obedience can be real fellowship with God.

sections.heading: Making me love people with the love of Jesus
sections.text: Spirit of love, grow your love in me and let it become visible in the way I treat people. Make me more like Jesus—not only in what I say I believe, but in the kindness I show, the good I do, the patience I practice, and the mercy I offer. Let people see something of your goodness in my life, so that the honor goes to you and not to me.
theological_themes: God’s love in the believer should become visible love toward others.
Christ is the pattern for Christian compassion and active goodness.
Good works are meant to glorify God, not the person doing them.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus commands his disciples to love one another as he has loved them and says this love will mark them as his disciples. This directly supports the prayer’s request to become loving in a recognizably Christlike way.
Jesus teaches that visible good works should lead others to glorify the Father. That fits the prayer’s desire for love and service to shine before others without stealing God’s honor.

sections.heading: Keeping me humble when you work through me
sections.text: And Father, the more you work in me and through me, the more humble I need to become. Do not let love make me proud, as if it came from me. Keep me gentle, low, teachable, and quick to give you the credit. If there is any good in me, it is your gift. If any good comes through me, it is your work. Let that truth keep me close to the ground and close to you.
theological_themes: Spiritual fruit should deepen humility, not pride.
All good in the believer comes from God’s grace and power.
God receives the honor for the love he produces in and through his people.

scripture_references.connection: Paul challenges boasting by reminding believers that everything they have is received. This supports the prayer’s refusal to take credit for love or usefulness that comes from God.
Paul says God works in believers both to will and to work for his good pleasure. That grounds the prayer’s confession that any loving desire or action is ultimately God’s work in the believer.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original’s statement that there is “by nature no pure love” in the soul reflects a strong Augustinian/Reformed view of sin and moral inability. I preserved that force while avoiding wording that would imply unbelievers never show any creaturely affection or civic good.

The original speaks of being a “slave to lust.” I rendered this broadly as bondage to disordered cravings, self-protection, pride, and comfort, because the older use of “lust” can mean more than sexual desire.
significant_interpretive_choices: I treated “means” as spiritual means or practices that are only fruitful when they lead the believer to God, rather than as a rejection of ordinary responsibilities or church practices.
I interpreted “happy converse with thee” as real fellowship with God through obedient response to his Word, not as an expectation of constant emotional happiness.
I kept the prayer in first person singular because the metadata identifies it as a personal private prayer.
